title: Chase Bank Transactions Disrupted by ‘Technical Issue’ Amid Outage Reports
summary: Chase was among several U.S. banks whose customers reported technical issues on Monday.
body_markdown:

Chase Bank, which serves more than 86 million customers at 5,000 branches across the United States, reported that it was having trouble processing transactions on Monday.


“Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,” the bank said in a statement. “We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.”


A Chase spokeswoman, Meghan Durant, said the bank was not having a “cyber issue.”


“We have no indication of bad actors,” she said.


Some Chase Bank customers reported on social media that they were unable to use their A.T.M. cards or complete transactions at branches on Monday.


Customers at several other major banks, including Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Bank of America, also reported problems on Monday, according to Downdetector.com, a website that tracks user reports of outages. Users also reported issues with the online payment platform Zelle.


U.S. Bank said in a statement that its “systems are not directly impacted.”


“However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” it said.


Zelle said it was “not down.”


“Zelle is operating as it should,” it said in a statement, which noted that customers who use the platform access their money through their own bank accounts. “An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” it said.


Wells Fargo and Bank of America did not immediately respond to requests for comment.


The banking issues were reported days after[a global outage at Microsoft](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/technology/microsoft-outage-what-to-know.html) disrupted communications and work at schools, government agencies, hospitals and offices around the world. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a[rare nationwide ground stop](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/faa-ground-stop-flights-what-to-know.html) after outdated air traffic communications equipment became overloaded and began to fail, officials said.


There was no indication that the bank issues on Monday were related to the outages at Microsoft. But the recent F.A.A. ground stop, which was related to an equipment problem with federal systems, added to the sense of gloom in social media chatter about troubles with modern technology.


The Microsoft outage, which started Thursday and was resolved on Saturday, affected some of its most popular products, including the email manager Outlook, the workplace messaging and video calling app Teams and the artificial intelligence assistant Copilot. Microsoft said the outage had been caused by a “technical issue” and not a cyberattack or A.I. agent.


The F.A.A. ground stop, which was lifted hours after it was issued on Friday, created a cascade of flight delays and cancellations that continued over the weekend. Government officials attributed the disarray to a[routine router upgrade](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/sean-duffy-ground-stop-trump-faa.html) at a radio facility in El Dorado, Ark. Workers also noticed a second unspecified issue at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas.


Michael Levenson covers breaking news for The Times from New York.
